newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: FEATURE - Mauritania heads for first budget surplus.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Mauritania heads for first budget surplus.

text.p: Mauritania, heading for its first budget surplus since independence from France in 1960, plans to join global efforts to stimulate world trade in January by lowering its tariff barriers.
The next step in the Moslem West African nation's programme to catch the eye of foreign investors is to update its commercial, mining and other laws.

But while the World Bank expresses satisfaction at government efforts to liberalise, privatise and improve the management of the economy, critics dispute the figures and say corruption and speculation are undermining the nation's wealth.

"Many investors say that as long as the legal system has not been revised they do not feel secure and that they cannot invest," Ahmed Ould Daddah, veteran opposition stalwart and former World Bank economist, told Reuters.
Ould Daddah has accused the authorities of widespread fraud in this month's legislative election which resulted in a landslide win for the ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party.
WORLD BANK APPROVES PROGRESS SO FAR
But while Ould Daddah and others are sceptical of the official figures, the World Bank, which is working closely wih the government, is pleased with the progress made.
"Mauritania is doing okay, particularly if you compare it with other countres in the region," says World Bank resident representative Claude Delapierre.
Growth was 4.5 percent in 1995 -- ahead of the World Bank global target of one percent after deducting a 2.9 percent population rise -- and inflation is under six percent.

"For the first time we will have a budget surplus this year," says Mohamed Ould Oumarou, adviser to the governor of the Central Bank. Figures for the first six months of 1996 point to a surplus of 1.2 percent, he adds.
Critics are sceptical. "You should be very wary of the figures, they can be made to show anything" says Ould Daddah.
BUDGET DISCIPLINE SUPPORTS CURRENCY

Oumarou says a tight government budget has kept Mauritania's ouguiya currency, devalued by 27 percent in 1992 but freely convertible since January, fairly stable. "We put up an extremely restrictive budget to keep the rate of the ouguiya fixed."
The government has also liberalised and privatised banks, of which there are five -- not counting the Central Bank.
The economy of Mauritania, which is at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara desert and straddles Arab and black Africa, relies on fishing, iron ore, agriculture and commerce.
"The trade balance has always been structurally positive," Delapierre says.
Figures for 1994 and 1995, and projections for 1996, show export income rising with the value of declared imports static.

Foreign exchange reserves almost doubled in 1995 to 61 million Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) and are projected to reach 117 million SDRs ($169 million) in 1996 -- enough to cover three months' imports.
Mauritania's foreign debt stands at about $2.3 billion, owed almost exclusively to the Paris Club of Western governments and to Arab and multilateral donors.
NO EARLY DEBT RELIEF
Delapierre said the structure of the debt meant Mauritania would not initially qualify for the debt forgiveness initiative agreed by international finance ministers last month.

He described domestic debt as negligible, with the fishing sector having negotiated a deal on 20 billion ouguiya ($145 million) it owed. The one remaining area of debt posing a problem concerned Air Mauritania, he added, declining to go into details.

The balance of payments, which fell from a deficit of 10 million SDRs in 1994 to four million in 1995 was projected to rise to eight million in 1996, due to fluctuations in capital movement, aid receipts and debt service payments, he said.

Oumarou said the goverment was now confident enough to lower tariff barriers. Starting in January the maximum customs duty will be 35 percent -- the current international target. At present, it ranges up to 148 percent for some luxury items.

The plan is to lower the maximum to 30 percent in 1998 and 28 percent in 1999. "The aim is to bring down prices," Oumarou said. VAT and other internal taxes would be used on luxury and other items to ensure investment reached key sectors.
NEW LAWS TO ATTRACT INVESTMENT

"Mauritania wants investment in profitable sectors such as fishing and agriculture," Oumarou said. The next stage is to redraft commercial and other law to ensure an attractive environment for investors. "We have liberalised. Now it's a question of redrafting the laws," he said, singling out commerce, mining and investment.

Delapierre said the project, which began in August, was designed to help Mauritania's government adapt and ensure a transparent framework providing equal opportunity for all. "It's a question of reforming mentalities, the way things are done."
Ould Daddah remains sceptical. He says says overfishing threatens stocks in Mauritania's traditionally rich waters.
Delapierre disagrees, citing an annual two-month moratorium in September and October, initiated this year.
Ould Daddah says speculation on land and unfair competition are compromising development of agriculture and business.
"This is a business-oriented country. Business is controlled by four men who are relatives of the head of state," he adds. "We have replaced a public monopoly by a private monopoly."
He and others say corruption is widespread. "There is a lot of expropriation and lot of overbilling," Ould Daddah said.
Delapierre is more sanguine. "There is fraud but it is not extremely significant," he said. ($1=138 ouguiya or 0.69 SDR)
